newsitem.title: UK: Bitter-sweet memories as Conservative era ends.
newsitem.headline: Bitter-sweet memories as Conservative era ends.

text.p: It was the best of times and it was the worst of times and it lasted for nearly two decades.
From 1979 to 1997, the Conservative Party under Margaret Thatcher and John Major oversaw a social revolution in Britain that left no-one indifferent and no-one unaffected.

Britain sent its army to the Falklands and won. But when the government sent police to battle rioters in Trafalgar Square it was forced to back down and abandon its new method of local government funding -- the reviled poll tax.

The unemployed, at one time more than three million of them, were told to "get on their bikes" and look for work, while yuppies working in financial markets earned breathtaking salaries and widespread scorn as they flaunted fast cars and champagne lifestyles.

Market forces were introduced into all areas of British life. Telecommunications, gas, water and electricity were among the utilities privatised, raising more than 70 billion pounds ($113 billion) for the government and turning millions of ordinary people into shareholders.

But economic dogma was taken to unpopular ends. The coal mining and steel industries were decimated. Attempts to privatise the railway system and introduce the market to the much-loved National Health Service caused uproar.

Many believed the Conservatives helped the rich get richer, particularly the "fat cats" of privatised industry, while the poor were left behind."Robin Hood has changed sides," said Labour MP Michael Meacher.

He said Britain's richest one percent enjoyed tax cuts worth more than 10 billion pounds since 1979. While for the poorest 50 percent, income tax cuts have been swallowed up by national insurance payments, Value Added Tax and other indirect taxes.

In the Thatcher heyday, the middle classes stepped over the homeless living in shop doorways on their way to dinner parties where gloating conversation turned on the apparently never-ending upward spiral in the value of their homes.
People marvelled that the value of their house had increased more in a month than the salaries they had to work for.

But house prices did come down, rather rapidly, as the 1980s became the 1990s. While Labour left its "loony left" past behind in the interests of becoming electable, the Conservatives tore themselves apart over Europe and paid the price at the polls.

Voters who had switched to Thatcher and rewarded her with victory when she promised them a foothold on the capitalist ladder turned against the Conservatives when their newly bought houses suddenly became worth less than their outstanding debt.

"Not everyone remembers how awful it was under Labour the last time," said Pamela Taylor, a long-time Conservative supporter, referring to a devastating series of strikes that helped Labour to lose power to Thatcher in 1979.
"They have forgotten the "winter of discontent', when the corpses were unburied and the streets were filled with rubbish."
The Conservatives bundled Thatcher out of office in 1990 as party chiefs, panicked by events like the poll tax riot, feared she had lost her grip and would lose them the 1992 election.
But Major was a grey image of the "Iron Lady" and was overshadowed once Tony Blair took over the Labour Party.

Supporters regard Thatcher with a kind of mystical fervour. But others revile her memory as a woman who centralised power by neutering local government, replaced consensus with conviction politics, and promoted "competitive individualism" at the expense of community and a sense of society.

"I will remember Thatcher as being as hard as nails with no compassion in her soul," said Karin Jensen, a part-time cleaning worker. Many feminists felt Thatcher's election would mark a turning point for women, but they were soon disillusioned.
The Iron Lady made no concessions to her sex. For her, the main criterion for advancement was to be "one of us" -- a reliable supporter of her policies and beliefs.
"At first I thought, great, a woman," said teacher Claire Cowley. "Then she started eroding women's rights, like maternity leave and nurseries. She seemed to erode everything for women."

Cowley conceded she was better off financially after 18 years of Conservative rule. But she worried about what happened to people who found themselves "downsized" out of jobs that had once seemed safe.
The children she taught often reflected the worries of their parents -- divorce and redundancy.
"Only middle-class kids get to go to university now because working class kids can't afford to repay student loans. If you slip off the greasy pole, you've had it," she said. ($1=.6175 Pound)
